1868-fundacao-da-loja-america.texto: The archive holds no minutes from this period: the surviving minutes begin on 26/08/1874. What is known comes from the plaque of Worshipful Masters and from references in later minutes: the founding on 9 November 1868, the constitution by the Warrant of 31/03/1869, the regularisation on 7/7/1869 and the Chapter Charter of 13/06/1874. According to the plaque, the first Worshipful Master was Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva (1868–1870), followed by Américo Brasiliense (1870–1872); twentieth-century minutes also record the tradition that Rui Barbosa, then a law student, was initiated in the Lodge on 5/7/1869.
1868-fundacao-da-loja-america.contexto: São Paulo was then a small provincial capital, enlivened by the Law School of Largo de São Francisco, which trained much of the Empire’s political elite. In 1868, in the midst of the Paraguayan War, the fall of Zacarias de Góis’s Liberal cabinet radicalised part of the Liberals and fed the republican movement, which would launch its Manifesto in 1870. In this setting, Masonic lodges were places of sociability and debate for students, journalists and politicians.
fotos: The old embroidered standard of the “Aug∴ and Resp∴ Chapter Lodge America”, with the founding date, 9 November 1868.

1869-regularizacao-no-grande-oriente-do.titulo: Regularisation in the Grand Orient of Brazil
1869-regularizacao-no-grande-oriente-do.texto: The Lodge, founded in 1868 by a group of professors and students of the Law School, was regularised on 07/07/1869 under the Grand Orient of Brazil (Valley of the Beneditinos) of Saldanha Marinho. According to the Lodge’s history, Joaquim Nabuco was initiated on 01/12/1868 and Rui Barbosa on 01/07/1869, both still students.
1869-regularizacao-no-grande-oriente-do.contexto: São Paulo was living through the academic and political agitation that followed the fall of the Liberal cabinet in July 1868; from this setting would come the Republican Party and the Itu Convention (1873).
detalhe: América Lodge was born on 9 November 1868, founded by eleven Brethren linked to the Law Academy of Largo de São Francisco, professors and students among them. The Lodge’s history lists among the founders Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva, Vicente Rodrigues da Silva, Inácio Aquiles Betoldi and Salvador Furtado de Mendonça Drummond.

On 7 July 1869 the Lodge was regularised in the Grand Orient of Brazil of the Valley of the Beneditinos, led by Joaquim Saldanha Marinho. In that first year two students were initiated who would become central figures in national life: Joaquim Nabuco, on 1 December 1868, and Rui Barbosa, on 1 July 1869.

In 1870 Américo Basílio de Campos, Luiz Gama and Américo Brasiliense de Almeida Melo joined, and they would shape the Lodge’s abolitionist and republican phase. According to the plaque of Worshipful Masters, Antonio Carlos led the Lodge from 1868 to 1870 and was succeeded by Américo Brasiliense (1870–1872). Vicente Rodrigues still appears in the earliest surviving minutes, elected Junior Warden in September 1874.

1870-ventre-livre-entre-os-irmaos.titulo: A free womb among the Brethren, a year before the law
1870-ventre-livre-entre-os-irmaos.texto: According to the Lodge’s history, in 1870 Rui Barbosa proposed in América’s temple that Brethren who were slaveholders should regard as free the children of enslaved women, a year before the Free Womb Law (28/09/1871). In the same year Américo de Campos (15/07), Luiz Gama (01/08) and Américo Brasiliense (22/08) joined the Lodge.
1870-ventre-livre-entre-os-irmaos.contexto: The Free Womb Law of 1871 declared free the children of enslaved women born from then on, but kept them under guardianship until the age of 21. The Lodge’s episode is a tradition recorded in its history and recalled at the solemn session of the City Council in 2008.
detalhe: In 1870, still a law student, Rui Barbosa put to the Lodge the proposal that Brethren who owned slaves should from that date regard as free the children born to enslaved women. The Lodge approved the idea, which anticipated the Free Womb Law (the Rio Branco Law of 28 September 1871) by a year. The Lodge was then passing from the term of Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva to that of Américo Brasiliense.

The proposal took shape in the bill of 4 April 1870, signed by Rui Barbosa and sent to the Grand Orient of Brazil, which came into force as law within América. In the text of the bill, the commitment required of the Brethren is to declare free the girls born to enslaved women (see the next item).

The abolitionist stance continued in the following decades and is recorded in the surviving minutes. In 1875 the Lodge receives the Grand Orient’s decree forbidding the initiation of anyone who traded in slaves. In 1876 it receives the decree allowing freedmen to be initiated. In 1879 and 1881 it collects alms for manumissions. In 1887 it agrees to initiate a candidate only after he frees his slaves, because “this Lodge is abolitionist”.

1870-escolas-noturnas-gratuitas.texto: On the initiative of Américo de Campos, in 1870–1871 the Lodge founded and ran free night and day schools, where political figures of the time taught. The Lodge’s tradition also credits it with the province’s first public library.
1870-escolas-noturnas-gratuitas.contexto: In a province with very high illiteracy, night schools for workers and freedmen were a cause of liberals, republicans and abolitionists.
detalhe: Under the leadership of Américo de Campos, in 1870 and 1871 the Lodge ran free day and night schools, open to workers and the poor, with volunteer teachers. According to the Lodge’s tradition, some of them were prominent figures in São Paulo politics. The Lodge is also remembered for founding the first public library in the province of São Paulo.

The minutes show the Night School, paid for by the Lodge, still running years later. In September 1874 the Lodge accepts 50 copies of the Apontamentos de Geographia e Cosmographia, compiled by Bro∴ Dr. Américo de Campos, for the pupils’ use. In 1875 Bro∴ Flaquer deals with the situation of the school’s assistant teacher. In 1881 the Lodge discusses who would teach the night classes and initiates a public schoolteacher with the fee exemption the Grand Orient granted to teachers.
papeis: organiser of the schools; author of the Apontamentos de Geographia
dealt with the Night School’s assistant teacher (1875)

1870-o-projeto-de-lei-de.texto: On 4 April 1870 América Lodge approved and sent to the Grand Orient of Brazil of the Valley of the Beneditinos a bill of Masonic law, signed by the young Brother Rui Barbosa, to oblige all Freemasonry in the country to work for the emancipation of the enslaved and for popular education. Each Lodge would set aside a fifth of its income to free children and would maintain free schools. No Mason could be initiated, or remain in the Order, without declaring free the girls born to women he held in slavery. Until the Grand Orient decided, the bill came into force as law within América itself.
1870-o-projeto-de-lei-de.contexto: In 1870 the Paraguayan War had just ended and the “question of the servile element”, raised by the Emperor in his Speech from the Throne of 1867, dominated political debate. Brazilian Freemasonry had been divided since 1863 into two Grand Orients: that of Lavradio, which had the Viscount of Rio Branco as Grand Master, and that of the Beneditinos, led by Joaquim Saldanha Marinho, which gathered liberals and republicans and to which América addressed itself. A year and a half later, Law No. 2,040 of 28 September 1871 (the Free Womb Law or Rio Branco Law) declared free the children of enslaved women born from then on, but left them under their masters’ authority until the age of 8 and, at the masters’ choice, in their service until 21.
detalhe: The author. Rui Barbosa was 20 and finishing his studies at the São Paulo Law Academy, from which he would graduate that same year. He had been initiated in América in July 1869, in a Lodge founded a year earlier by professors and students of the Academy, which brought together much of the city’s liberal and abolitionist youth. Luiz Gama, Américo de Campos and Américo Brasiliense were members. The bill was presented as the Lodge passed from the term of Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva to that of Américo Brasiliense, whom the plaque of Worshipful Masters records for 1870–1872.

The request. The Lodge submitted the text “to the wise consideration of the Gr∴ Or∴ of the Valley of the Beneditinos”, asking that it become “a general and binding law for all Freemasonry established in the country”. It was a proposal for the whole Order, not an isolated gesture: if approved, every Lodge of the Grand Orient would have to adopt the two principles in order to remain regular and legitimate.

The two great ideas. Article 1 declares that the emancipation of the servile element and popular education are “two great ideas that stir the public spirit” and on which the nation’s future depends. Freemasonry would commit itself to defending them through the press, the rostrum and teaching, and with material resources as well. Article 2 makes these principles a condition for a Lodge to be recognised as regular.

Money and schools. Article 3 obliges each Lodge to set aside in its budget a special fund, always equal to one fifth of its total income, to buy the freedom of enslaved children. It also obliges Lodges to create free primary schools: night or Sunday schools for adults “of all classes” and day schools for children “of both sexes”. América itself put this part of the bill into practice: in 1870 and 1871, on the initiative of Américo de Campos, it ran free night and day schools, and the minutes show the Night School still running in 1874 and 1875.

Each Brother’s commitment. The boldest point is in Articles 5 to 7. No candidate could be initiated without first declaring free all the girls born thereafter to women he held in slavery. Masons already initiated would have to sign the same commitment. The declarations would be written and signed by each Brother, one per page, with witnesses, in a numbered and initialled book, so that they would have legal force outside the Lodge. Under the rule of the time, slave status passed from mother to children. By freeing the girls, the bill cut this transmission in the next generation.

The sanctions. Anyone refusing to sign would not be initiated or, if already a Mason, would be suspended throughout Brazilian Freemasonry (Art. 8). Anyone who signed and still kept the children in captivity would be expelled from the Order, losing all titles and dignities (Art. 9). The Lodge would also have to appoint someone to prosecute the offender in the civil courts, using the commitment itself as evidence, until a judgment of freedom for the children was obtained (Art. 10). A Lodge that failed to comply would be reprimanded and, if it resisted, suspended (Art. 11).

Immediate law in América. Article 12 provides that, until the Grand Orient decided, all these provisions would apply “from today as positive law within the Lodge América”. América’s Brethren who held slaves were therefore bound by the commitment from 4 April 1870. The digitised archive of minutes begins in 1874 and does not record the Grand Orient’s reply.

Compared with the law of 1871. América’s bill freed only the girls, whereas the Free Womb Law freed boys and girls alike. In other respects, however, it was more demanding: freedom took effect immediately, without the years of service to the master provided for in the law; it was overseen by the Lodge and could be enforced in the courts. It also came with funds for manumissions and schools for the freed.

The meaning of the document. According to the commentary published on the Lodge’s website, the bill shows that América defended emancipation, not a mere “general manumission”: freeing without educating would be useless, because the freed needed the means to truly exercise their freedom and take part in society as equals. Later, realising that gradualism mainly served to prolong slavery, the Lodge moved to the line of Luiz Gama and Antônio Bento, with organised escapes and support for the Quilombo do Jabaquara (see the items for 1875, 1881 and 1882).

1874-luiz-gama-e-eleito-veneravel.titulo: Luiz Gama is elected Worshipful Master
1874-luiz-gama-e-eleito-veneravel.texto: In the first surviving minutes, Luiz Gonzaga Pinto da Gama is elected Worshipful Master with 17 of 18 ballots, and Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva and Américo Brasiliense are acclaimed Honorary Worshipful Masters. Gama would be re-elected year after year and, in August 1877, received from the Supreme Council the 33rd degree, the highest of the Scottish Rite. Under his leadership the Lodge brought together names from São Paulo’s abolitionist and republican circle, such as Américo de Campos.
1874-luiz-gama-e-eleito-veneravel.contexto: Luiz Gama (1830–1882) was born free in Bahia and illegally sold into slavery as a boy. In São Paulo he won his freedom, learned to read and became a self-taught lawyer and journalist, obtaining in court the freedom of hundreds of enslaved people. He is recognised today as one of the greatest names of Brazilian abolitionism.

1874-uma-esmola-pela-liberdade-de.texto: At a session presided over by Luiz Gama, the Lodge approves alms of 20$000 “towards the freedom of Umbelina, a slave of the estate of Alexandrina C. de Carvalho”. It is the first record in the minutes of Lodge money used to buy the freedom of an enslaved person. Similar requests would appear again in 1879 and 1881.
1874-uma-esmola-pela-liberdade-de.contexto: Before Abolition, one way of freeing an enslaved person was to pay the owner the price of manumission. The Free Womb Law of 1871 recognised the right of the enslaved to build up savings to buy their own freedom, and associations, brotherhoods and Masonic lodges began raising funds for this purpose.

1874-a-loja-na-questao-religiosa.titulo: The Lodge in the Religious Question
1874-a-loja-na-questao-religiosa.texto: The Lodge receives the Grand Master’s decree on the defence of Masonic rights “disregarded by the ultramontane clergy” and arranges for a power of attorney to be signed in the Grand Master’s favour. In 1875 it receives the writings of “Ganganelli” on the Religious Question and is approached by a lodge in Ribeirão Preto denouncing persecution by local authorities. At the same time, the minutes show the Lodge running a night school.
1874-a-loja-na-questao-religiosa.contexto: The Religious Question (1872–1875) set the Church against the imperial government: the bishops of Olinda and Pará forbade Catholic brotherhoods to keep Masons as members, were tried and sentenced to prison in 1874 and pardoned in 1875. “Ganganelli” was the pen name of Joaquim Saldanha Marinho, Grand Master and a liberal and republican leader. The episode deepened the friction between the Empire and the Church.

1875-irmaos-da-america-fundam-a.titulo: Brethren of América found A Província de São Paulo
1875-irmaos-da-america-fundam-a.texto: On 4 January 1875 the first issue of A Província de São Paulo, today O Estado de S. Paulo, came out, founded with republican ideas by Masons, among them Américo de Campos and Francisco Rangel Pestana of América Lodge. In the same issue, a column on public instruction credited América with being first to create schools maintained by private initiative.
1875-irmaos-da-america-fundam-a.contexto: At the time, almost all education was in the hands of religious orders or fee-paying schools, and the imperial government maintained very few public schools. Illiteracy was almost universal.
detalhe: According to an article by José Castellani reproduced on the Lodge’s website, A Província de São Paulo was founded in 1875 by the Masons Américo de Campos and Francisco Rangel Pestana, of América Lodge, Manoel Ferraz de Campos Salles, of Loja Sete de Setembro, and José Maria Lisboa, of Loja Amizade. The newspaper would become O Estado de S. Paulo.

In the issue of 4 January 1875, the “Public instruction” column praised the enthusiasm for education in the province and stated that América Lodge deserved the credit for being first in this praiseworthy undertaking, having been the first to proclaim, and to show by deeds, that the people must take charge of their own instruction directly.

For the Lodge, public education was part of the same plan as the emancipation of the enslaved and the establishment of a democratic republic. América’s schools were supported by the Brethren themselves.

1875-fechada-a-traficantes-aberta-a.titulo: Closed to slave traders, open to freedmen
1875-fechada-a-traficantes-aberta-a.texto: The Lodge receives the decree of the United Grand Orient forbidding the initiation of anyone who trades in slaves and declares it “in harmony with the thinking” of its members. In September 1876 it receives another decree, under which freedmen, “by the fact of having been born slaves”, are not excluded from initiation. In this period the Lodge also faced a financial crisis, which Luiz Gama tried to resolve with a plan for collecting and forgiving debts.
1875-fechada-a-traficantes-aberta-a.contexto: The African slave trade to Brazil had been banned in 1850, but the internal trade in enslaved people, above all from the Northeast to the coffee farms of the Southeast, remained intense. Traditional Masonic constitutions required candidates to be “free” men, which in a slave society raised the question of admitting freedmen.

1877-inauguracao-de-um-novo-templo.texto: In March 1875 the owner of the house where the Lodge met demanded it back because the building threatened to collapse, and the Lodge launched a share subscription to buy premises of its own. In October 1876 it decided to move to Mr Lima’s house; Luiz Gama pointed out that lodges could not sign contracts because they had no legal personality. The first session in the new temple, decorated by a committee of Gama, Amaral and Jesuino de Castro, took place on 6/2/1877.
1877-inauguracao-de-um-novo-templo.contexto: Under the Empire, Masonic lodges had no legal existence as corporate bodies, so property and contracts were held in members’ names. For decades América Lodge would share its temple with other lodges in the capital, such as Sete de Setembro, a common practice among lodges of modest means.

1881-conferencias-noturnas-e-ensino-popu.texto: The Lodge unanimously approves José Leão’s proposal to organise evening instruction lectures, with a committee formed by Luiz Gama, Leão and Silva Jardim. In June a plan is presented for a primary-education section and scientific talks. Public schoolteachers were encouraged to join without paying the admission fee, under a Grand Orient decree.
1881-conferencias-noturnas-e-ensino-popu.contexto: At the end of the Empire most of Brazil’s population was illiterate and public schools were scarce. Masons, republicans and abolitionists saw popular education as a path to citizenship, and many lodges ran schools and evening courses for workers.

1881-projeto-de-emancipacao-com-silva.titulo: An emancipation plan, with Silva Jardim in the Lodge
1881-projeto-de-emancipacao-com-silva.texto: A plan of measures “to emancipate the man reduced to slavery” is read in the Lodge, with a favourable opinion signed by José Leão and Luiz Gama; the debate of 15/07 divided the Brethren and was adjourned. Among those who spoke was Antonio da Silva Jardim, initiated in May 1881. In May, the minutes also mention a Brother whose slaves had been freed on the Lodge’s initiative.
1881-projeto-de-emancipacao-com-silva.contexto: In the early 1880s abolitionism became a mass campaign, with newspapers, lectures and associations in several cities. Antônio da Silva Jardim (1860–1891) would become one of the most fiery propagandists of the Republic. Luiz Gama died in August 1882 without seeing Abolition.

1882-fugas-de-escravizados-e-o.titulo: Escapes of the enslaved and the Quilombo do Jabaquara
1882-fugas-de-escravizados-e-o.texto: According to the Lodge’s history, América promoted escapes of enslaved people together with Antonio Bento’s Caifazes (Loja Piratininga) and Brethren of Loja Ypiranga, and helped support the Quilombo do Jabaquara in Santos, which by the time of the Golden Law would shelter more than ten thousand people.
1882-fugas-de-escravizados-e-o.contexto: In the 1880s São Paulo abolitionism moved from propaganda to direct action: mass escapes from the plantations and refuge in Santos, a city that became a symbol of freedom. The exact dates of this activity are not recorded in the archived minutes.
detalhe: In the 1880s the Lodge moved from propaganda to direct action. According to its history, it organised escapes of enslaved people with Antonio Bento’s Caifazes, of Loja Piratininga, and with Brethren of Loja Ypiranga. It also helped create and support the Quilombo do Jabaquara in Santos, which on the eve of the Golden Law sheltered more than ten thousand people.

Luiz Gama, elected Worshipful Master in 1874 and again in 1880–1881, was the great voice of this movement until his death on 24 August 1882. The minutes record the mood of the time. In 1880 the Lodge proposes to defend press freedom against advertisements for “runaway slaves and slaves for sale”. In 1881 Bro∴ Passos speaks about the slave and presents the plea of a mother begging alms to free her daughter.

1886-amparo-a-viuva-de-luiz.texto: On leaving the Lodge, Worshipful Master Lobo Peçanha sends 200$000, asking that half go to Luiz Gama’s widow and the rest to the fund for enslaved Brethren or to the poor. In 1890 the Lodge unanimously approves a monthly pension of 15$000 for the widow, calling Gama a former Worshipful Master, and the pension was still being paid in 1900. In 1901 Gama’s son thanked the Lodge for what it had done for his mother.
1886-amparo-a-viuva-de-luiz.contexto: Charity is one of the pillars of Freemasonry: lodges kept relief funds to help sick Brethren, widows and orphans. The care for Luiz Gama’s family, kept up for more than fifteen years, also shows how the Lodge cherished the memory of its most celebrated Worshipful Master.

1887-esta-oficina-e-abolicionista.texto: The Lodge makes the initiation of a candidate who owned slaves conditional on his freeing them first, because “this Lodge is abolitionist”. The decision was taken eight months before the Golden Law. In the same period the Lodge was going through an internal electoral dispute, taken to the Grand Lodge.
1887-esta-oficina-e-abolicionista.contexto: In 1887 slavery was collapsing in São Paulo: mass escapes from the plantations, supported by Antonio Bento’s “caifazes”, and the Army’s refusal to hunt fugitives made the system unsustainable. The Sexagenarian Law (1885) had freed only enslaved people over 60.

1888-a-loja-italia-ganha-abrigo.titulo: Loja Italia finds a home in the temple
1888-a-loja-italia-ganha-abrigo.texto: The Lodge unanimously agrees that Loja Italia may work in its temple on the same terms as Sete de Setembro, at the request of Jesuino Antonio de Castro, who sat on the committee regularising the new lodge. The idea of an Italian Lodge in São Paulo had come up at an América session in December 1887.
1888-a-loja-italia-ganha-abrigo.contexto: From the mid-1880s, subsidised immigration brought tens of thousands of Italians to São Paulo, to the coffee farms and to the city. The Italian presence would strongly mark São Paulo Freemasonry and América Lodge’s own membership in the following decades.

1888-a-loja-celebra-a-abolicao.texto: Eight days after the Golden Law, at an extraordinary session, the Lodge approves a vote of praise to Rangel Pestana, Américo de Campos, Américo Brasiliense, Antonio Carlos and Saldanha Marinho for the “complete extinction of slavery”. It buys wreaths for Luiz Gama’s tomb and in honour of José Bonifácio, carried in the civic procession, and sends congratulations to Antonio Bento.
1888-a-loja-celebra-a-abolicao.contexto: The Golden Law of 13 May 1888 abolished slavery in Brazil without compensation to owners and without measures to integrate the freed. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

1889-nasce-na-america-a-grande.titulo: The Grand Lodge of São Paulo is born in América
1889-nasce-na-america-a-grande.texto: Caetano Nacarato, Arthur Campos and Joaquim Soares obtain unanimous authorisation to work towards founding a Provincial Grand Lodge, arguing that the Grand Orient in Rio cared little for the lodges in the provinces. In August the Lodge thanks Nacarato as the initiator of the Provincial Grand Lodge of São Paulo, by then regularised, and Worshipful Master Américo de Campos states that it was América that started the movement.
1889-nasce-na-america-a-grande.contexto: Brazilian Freemasonry was run from Rio de Janeiro, the imperial capital. The São Paulo lodges’ wish for autonomy went hand in hand with the economic growth of the coffee province and the federalist demands of the São Paulo republicans.

1889-adesao-a-republica.texto: A week after 15 November, the Lodge unanimously approves a motion by Américo de Campos hailing the republican regime as a “guarantee of Liberty and Tolerance”, communicated to the Provisional Government of São Paulo through Rangel Pestana. In March 1890 it records the installation of Generalissimo Deodoro da Fonseca as Grand Master and the farewell of Américo de Campos, who was leaving the country on a mission for the new government.
1889-adesao-a-republica.contexto: The Republic was proclaimed on 15 November 1889 by a military movement led by Deodoro da Fonseca, who headed the Provisional Government and in 1890 also became Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Brazil. São Paulo republicans, many of them Masons, took prominent positions in the new regime.

1889-enfermeiras-para-a-epidemia-de.texto: During the serious epidemic that struck Santos in 1889, the Lodge organised and supported a team of nurses, according to its history.
1889-enfermeiras-para-a-epidemia-de.contexto: Yellow fever epidemics had been ravaging Santos, the coffee port, since the end of the 1880s, killing thousands.
detalhe: In 1889 Santos faced one of the worst epidemics in its history, of yellow fever. According to the Lodge’s traditional history, América organised and paid for a team of nurses sent to the city to care for the sick.

This account has not preserved the names of the nurses or of the Brethren in charge, and the transcribed minutes of 1889 do not mention the action. That year the Lodge was led by Antônio Archanjo Dias Baptista and, from the 1889 elections, by Américo de Campos.

1893-a-america-lidera-a-criacao.titulo: América leads the creation of the first Grand Orient of São Paulo
1893-a-america-lidera-a-criacao.texto: On 28 May 1893, under the leadership of América Lodge and of Martim Francisco Ribeiro de Andrada III, the Grand Orient of São Paulo was created, autonomous from the Grand Orient of Brazil. It was one of the first Masonic organisations in the country to register its statutes, as required by Decree No. 173 of 10/09/1893.
1893-a-america-lidera-a-criacao.contexto: Decree No. 173 of 10 September 1893 required the registration of all religious, charitable and political societies, including Masonic Obediences and Lodges. São Paulo Freemasonry was divided between the new Grand Orient and the State Grand Lodge, loyal to the GOB.
detalhe: According to an article by José Castellani reproduced on the Lodge’s website, Martim Francisco’s Grand Orient initially brought together the Lodges América, which had led the movement, Roma, União Paulista, Sete de Setembro, Vinte de Setembro and Harmonia e Caridade, joined by Amizade in September. Loja Piratininga stayed with the Grand Orient of Brazil.

The new Grand Orient and Loja Amizade were the first Brazilian Masonic organisations to comply with Decree No. 173, registering their statutes in the State Official Gazette of 9 October 1894. The Grand Orient of Brazil registered its Constitution only on 25 October 1895. For the Lodge’s website, the gesture confirmed América’s commitment to the republican ideal: the laws apply to everyone, without exception or privilege.
América’s minutes for this period (1891–1896) are not in the digitised archive. The defence of the São Paulo Grand Orient reappears in the minutes of 1898.
papeis: leader of the movement; Worshipful Master of the Lodge

1894-basta-de-sangue-a-pacificacao.titulo: “Enough blood”: the pacification of the South
1894-basta-de-sangue-a-pacificacao.texto: According to the Lodge’s history, it was América that proposed giving full powers to the Grand Master to seek in Rio de Janeiro the pacification of Rio Grande do Sul. Before that, the Lodge had intervened to prevent the execution by firing squad of Brother Isidoro Fernandes, a prisoner of the rebels.
1894-basta-de-sangue-a-pacificacao.contexto: The Federalist Revolution (1893–1895) set federalists against Castilhista republicans in the South, with thousands of dead and throat-cutting of prisoners, and ended with the peace of August 1895.
detalhe: The Federalist Revolution (1893–1895) set federalists against republicans in Rio Grande do Sul and spread to Santa Catarina and Paraná, with thousands of dead and executions of prisoners. Between 1894 and 1895 the Lodge proposed to Freemasonry that the Grand Master be given full powers to negotiate the pacification of the South. The Lodge’s position was: whatever it takes, enough blood.

Before that, the Lodge had already intervened to prevent the execution of Bro∴ Isidoro Fernandes, a prisoner of the rebels. According to the plaque, the Worshipful Master in those years was Caetano Nacarato, who led the Lodge from 1890 to 1905.

1896-os-protocolos-italianos.texto: During the 1896 clashes in São Paulo linked to the so-called Italian Protocols, the Lodge telegraphed the Grand Master in Santos asking for Masonic intervention for public order; according to its history, the disturbances stopped six days later.
1896-os-protocolos-italianos.contexto: The protocols negotiated between Brazil and Italy to compensate Italians who had suffered losses provoked riots and clashes between students, nationalists and Italian immigrants in the city of São Paulo in 1896.
detalhe: In 1896 news of the Italian Protocols, the agreement to compensate Italian citizens harmed in Brazil, provoked street fighting between Brazilians and Italian immigrants in São Paulo. The Lodge telegraphed the Grand Master of Freemasonry, who was in Santos, asking for Masonic intervention to restore order. Six days later calm had returned.

The initiative had a particular meaning for América: the minutes of the decade show many Italian immigrants among those initiated and ties with Loja Itália, to whose installation the Lodge sent a committee in 1890. The Worshipful Master was Caetano Nacarato.

1897-contra-o-atentado-a-prudente.titulo: Against the attack on Prudente de Morais
1897-contra-o-atentado-a-prudente.texto: On the very day of the attack, the Lodge approves a motion of condemnation and grief at the murder of Marshal Carlos Machado Bittencourt, Minister of War, “in an attack aimed at the Head of the Nation”, and asks the Grand Master to speak out. At the next session, Nacarato reports that the Grand Master telegraphed condolences to the Federal Capital.
1897-contra-o-atentado-a-prudente.contexto: On 5 November 1897, in Rio de Janeiro, a soldier tried to kill President Prudente de Morais, the Republic’s first civilian president; the Minister of War died defending him. The attack came just after the end of the Canudos War, in a climate of sharp political radicalisation.

1898-federalismo-maconico-a-defesa-do.titulo: Masonic federalism: defending the São Paulo Grand Orient
1898-federalismo-maconico-a-defesa-do.texto: The Lodge refuses to let a member join a lodge linked to the Grand Orient in Rio, stating that it represents unitarism, “something that no longer exists in Brazil”, while São Paulo’s represents federation. In 1901 Worshipful Master Caetano Nacarato denounces as a “fraud” Grand Master Quintino Bocayuva’s decree creating a parallel Grand Orient in São Paulo, and the Lodge approves a solemn protest. The minutes refer to the Grand Orient of São Paulo as a work in which América played a central role.
1898-federalismo-maconico-a-defesa-do.contexto: The Constitution of 1891 adopted federalism, giving the states great autonomy. In Freemasonry, the Grand Orient of São Paulo, organised in 1893, claimed independence from the Grand Orient of Brazil in Rio, in a conflict between obediences that would recur throughout the twentieth century.

1902-morre-o-primeiro-veneravel.texto: Funeral minutes record the death of Dr. Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva, “first Worshipful Master of the Lodge”, Honorary Worshipful Master for life and Deputy Grand Master when “we made the Gr∴ Or∴ of São Paulo”, and of former Worshipful Master Antonio Archanjo Dias Baptista. After these minutes the archive has a gap until 1916; for that interval only the plaque indicates the Worshipful Masters.
1902-morre-o-primeiro-veneravel.contexto: Antonio Carlos Ribeiro de Andrada Machado e Silva belonged to the Andrada family of José Bonifácio, one of the most traditional in São Paulo politics. Gaps in lodge archives are common: in 1968 the Lodge itself attributed part of its documentary losses to the destruction of papers kept by private individuals.

1917-a-beira-de-fechar-as.titulo: On the verge of closing its doors
1917-a-beira-de-fechar-as.texto: Secretary Caetano Nacarato explains that, with no initiations for many years and dues in arrears, the Lodge risks “lowering its columns” for failing to pay the rent. The Brethren take on monthly contributions and make donations to keep the Lodge open. In 1916 the Secretary himself had already recorded that the Lodge, for its deeds on behalf of the nation’s liberties, deserved more respect from the Brethren.
1917-a-beira-de-fechar-as.contexto: The years of the First World War (1914–1918) brought high prices and social unrest to São Paulo, which saw a large general strike in July 1917. Many of the city’s traditional associations lost members and resources in this period.

1919-fusao-com-a-fratellanza-universale.texto: At a grand session, the Lodges América and Fratellanza Universale merge, keeping the name América and making Caetano Nacarato, promoter of the union who had died in November 1918, Honorary Worshipful Master. The merger, approved on 22/11/1918, renewed the Lodge’s membership. Soon after, the Lodge approved a reorganisation programme with a school, a library, a newspaper and a burial vault.
1919-fusao-com-a-fratellanza-universale.contexto: Mergers were a frequent solution for lodges with few members. The end of the First World War in November 1918 and the Spanish flu, which hit São Paulo the same year, marked the moment the Lodge reorganised.

1919-causa-operaria-e-defesa-de.titulo: The workers’ cause and the defence of Everardo Dias
1919-causa-operaria-e-defesa-de.texto: On 13 May 1919 the Lodge publicly celebrated its role in Abolition and the Worshipful Master defended the workers’ demands. In December it approved a protest against the arrest and deportation of the journalist and labour activist Everardo Dias, who had joined the Lodge in July 1919, accusing a Masonic Supreme Court justice of betraying his oath by denying habeas corpus; it also approved protests against foreign intervention in Russia and against the Gordo Law. In 1920 it welcomed Everardo’s return; he argued that the Lodge, promoter of Abolition and of the Republic, should not stand aside from the social question.
1919-causa-operaria-e-defesa-de.contexto: Between 1917 and 1920 Brazil went through a wave of strikes inspired by anarchism and the Russian Revolution of 1917. The Adolfo Gordo Law allowed foreigners deemed dangerous to be expelled and was used against labour leaders. In Russia, foreign powers intervened in the civil war between 1918 and 1920.

1921-da-america-ao-grao-mestrado.titulo: From América to the São Paulo Grand Mastership
1921-da-america-ao-grao-mestrado.texto: Several Brethren of América led São Paulo Freemasonry. The most notable is José Adriano Marrey Júnior, the Lodge’s Orator in 1919, who led the founding of the Grand Orient of São Paulo on 29/07/1921 and was its Grand Master until 1942. Aurélio de Souza, Worshipful Master of América, was Grand Master of the GOSP from 1962 to 1964.
1921-da-america-ao-grao-mestrado.contexto: The Grand Orient of São Paulo was born in 1921 from the separation of São Paulo’s Lodges from the Grand Orient of Brazil. It rejoined the GOB in 1929, left in 1973, returned in 1980 and left the federation again in 2018.
detalhe: América’s link with the leadership of São Paulo Freemasonry is long-standing. In 1893, according to the Lodge’s history, it was América, with Martim Francisco Ribeiro de Andrada III, that led the first Grand Orient of São Paulo. Pedro de Toledo, also a Brother of the Lodge, was Grand Master of the State Grand Orient from 1908 to 1914.

José Adriano Marrey Júnior was elected Orator of América in May 1919. That same year the Lodge was the first to launch his candidacy for state deputy, “as he was a rare Mason who defended the Masonic cause”, and appointed a committee to congratulate him when he took office. Already state Grand Master, he presided over a grand session of the Lodge in January 1921. On 29 July 1921, after his address, most of the State’s Lodges separated from the Grand Orient of Brazil, and América joined the Grand Orient of São Paulo, which Marrey Júnior led until 1942.

Aurélio de Souza joined América in 1951, was the Lodge’s Orator and Worshipful Master and, according to the GOSP gallery, Grand Master from 1962 to 1964. In January 1963, as Grand Master, he visited the Lodge, spoke about modernising the Order and supported the candidacies of Álvaro Palmeira and Erasmo Martins Pedro for the national Grand Mastership. Palmeira would be the reformer of the Brazilian Rite, which América would adopt in 1969.
More recently, Benedito Marques Ballouk Filho, an Honorary Member of the Lodge according to the Sesquicentennial plaque, was Grand Master of the GOSP in 2007–2011, 2015–2018 and 2020–2024.

1921-a-cisao-duas-lojas-america.texto: After most São Paulo lodges decided on 29/07/1921 to separate from the Grand Orient of Brazil, the Lodge split in two: one group, on Rua Xavier de Toledo, joined the Grand Orient of São Paulo under João Gallo; another, meeting at Rua Carlos Gomes, 50, stayed loyal to the GOB and expelled the dissidents. The two factions disputed the temple fund, the archive and the standard, which Gallo’s group recovered in October 1922.
1921-a-cisao-duas-lojas-america.contexto: Disputes between the Grand Orient of Brazil and state Powers marked Brazilian Freemasonry in the twentieth century. The São Paulo separation of 1921 repeated the federalist argument of 1893 and was only overcome with the unification agreements at the end of the 1920s.

1922-o-levante-de-julho-e.titulo: The July uprising and the centenary of Independence
1922-o-levante-de-julho-e.texto: Faced with the country’s “most distressing situation” in the days of the uprising of 5 July 1922, the Lodge approves a vote of confidence in its members “for the sake of order, legality, liberty and justice”, without party character. At the same session, Amadeu Amaral is asked to write the Lodge’s historical account for the Masonic Album of the centenary of Independence. In 1924 the Lodge would agree to work for an amnesty for the rebels of 1922.
1922-o-levante-de-julho-e.contexto: On 5 July 1922 young officers rebelled at Copacabana Fort against the government, starting the tenentista movement. The year 1922 also marked the centenary of Independence and the Modern Art Week in São Paulo.

1923-luto-por-rui-barbosa.texto: The Lodge holds a session of mourning for the death of Rui Barbosa, “great workman of this Lodge”, and the Secretary recalls his initiation on 5/7/1869, when he was a law student. At a solemn funeral session presided over by the Grand Master, Rui’s portrait is placed in the temple. From then on, Rui Barbosa becomes a constant presence in the memory the Lodge cultivates of itself.
1923-luto-por-rui-barbosa.contexto: Rui Barbosa (1849–1923), jurist, politician and diplomat, studied law in São Paulo at the end of the 1860s. He was Minister of Finance in the Provisional Government, one of the authors of the 1891 Constitution and Brazil’s representative at the Hague Conference of 1907.

1923-memoria-da-convencao-de-itu.texto: As the fiftieth anniversary of the Itu Convention approaches, the Lodge visits Senator José Luiz Flaquer, a former member and surviving delegate. Flaquer recounts that the preparatory meeting of 24/12/1872 was to have been held in América’s temple but, because of government surveillance, took place at the house of Américo de Campos, and that the Lodge obtained the freedom of 200 slaves belonging to a commander from Santos. The Lodge regrets having been forgotten in the official celebrations.
1923-memoria-da-convencao-de-itu.contexto: The Itu Convention of 18 April 1873 gathered planters, lawyers and journalists and gave rise to the São Paulo Republican Party, the best-organised republican party of the Empire. Many of its members were Masons.

1923-solidariedade-aos-macons-italianos-.titulo: Solidarity with Italian Masons under fascism
1923-solidariedade-aos-macons-italianos-.texto: The Lodge approves a letter of solidarity with Italian Masons persecuted by fascism and, in 1924 and 1925, protests against the burning of Masonic temples in Italy. In 1925 the proposal for the Masonic Club of the State of São Paulo, against Mussolini’s persecution of Masons, is born in the Lodge. From 1926 the Lodge called for fascists to be removed from the Order, and in 1929 it applauded a proposal to that effect, because “no fascist can be a Mason”.
1923-solidariedade-aos-macons-italianos-.contexto: Benito Mussolini came to power in Italy in 1922. The fascist regime attacked Masonic lodges and in 1925 passed a law against secret associations that led to the dissolution of Italian Freemasonry. In São Paulo, with its large Italian community, clashes between fascists and anti-fascists spilled onto the streets.

1924-a-revolta-paulista-de-1924.texto: Worshipful Master João Gallo reports that during the revolt of July 1924 he gathered the Lodge at his home to help Brethren in need and offered, on its behalf, 200$000 to the committee collecting donations for the victims, a gesture unanimously approved. In 1925 one Brother lamented in the minutes the “atmosphere of terror” in the country and another asked: “What is Freemasonry doing, that it does not react?”.
1924-a-revolta-paulista-de-1924.contexto: On 5 July 1924 tenentista officers occupied the city of São Paulo for more than three weeks; the city was bombarded by federal forces and hundreds died. Artur Bernardes’s government (1922–1926) ruled much of its term under a state of siege.

1930-templo-na-praca-da-se.titulo: A temple on Praça da Sé
1930-templo-na-praca-da-se.texto: After leaving Rua Xavier de Toledo, the Lodge met on Rua José Bonifácio (1926) and Rua Conde do Pinhal (1926–1929). On 8/1/1930 it inaugurated its temple in the Palacete Piratininga, at Praça da Sé, 26. At the opening session, a visitor blamed the country’s crisis on “petty politics” and said that only Freemasonry could prevent a catastrophe that might even lead to civil war.
1930-templo-na-praca-da-se.contexto: Praça da Sé was the heart of a São Paulo that was growing vertically in the 1920s and 1930s. The year 1930 began under the impact of the 1929 crash, which brought down the price of coffee, and of the presidential dispute that would lead to the Revolution of 1930.

1930-centenario-de-luiz-gama-e.titulo: Luiz Gama’s centenary and Masonic unification
1930-centenario-de-luiz-gama-e.texto: The Lodge honours Luiz Gama on the centenary of his birth, recalling that it initiated him and raised a mausoleum to him in the Consolação Cemetery. At the same session the circular on the unification of the Grand Orient of São Paulo with the Grand Orient of Brazil is read, and three days later the installation minutes record that “the unification of Freemasonry in Brazil is done”. In August the Lodge founded its Library.
1930-centenario-de-luiz-gama-e.contexto: Brazilian Freemasonry, divided since 1921, negotiated reunification in congresses and agreements between 1926 and 1930. The memory of Luiz Gama, who died in 1882, was kept alive by the Lodge’s annual tributes at his tomb.

1930-a-revolucao-de-1930.texto: In August the Lodge voted its grief at the murder of João Pessoa. At the first session after work was suspended because of the political situation, the Worshipful Master reports having helped Brethren with money and letters of recommendation, and announces that a Brother detained during the events was free. The Orator appealed for peace and order.
1930-a-revolucao-de-1930.contexto: The murder in July 1930 of João Pessoa, president of Paraíba and the defeated vice-presidential candidate, precipitated the armed movement that in October deposed Washington Luís and brought Getúlio Vargas to power at the head of a Provisional Government.

1931-o-manifesto-da-loja-america.texto: The Lodge unanimously approves a manifesto to the Masons of Brazil, drafted from a proposal by Paulo de Gusmão: it calls for a return to constitutional rule, a new electoral law, a constituent assembly within six months and the end of the Special Revolutionary Tribunal, and defends secular education and civil marriage. It then proposes a central committee for keeping Article 72 of the 1891 Constitution, and lodges in other states express their solidarity. At the same time, consulted by a lodge in Campinas, the Lodge voted 11 to 4 against women’s right to vote.
1931-o-manifesto-da-loja-america.contexto: Vargas’s Provisional Government dissolved Congress, appointed intervenors in the states and in April 1931 reintroduced religious teaching in public schools, bringing State and Church closer again. Women’s suffrage would be introduced by the Electoral Code of February 1932.

1932-a-frente-negra-brasileira-honra.titulo: The Brazilian Black Front honours Luiz Gama and Antônio Bento
1932-a-frente-negra-brasileira-honra.texto: On 13 May 1932 the Brazilian Black Front celebrated Abolition with a mass, a gathering at its headquarters on Rua da Liberdade and the traditional visit to the tombs of Luiz Gama, José Bonifácio the Younger and Antônio Bento in the Consolação Cemetery.
1932-a-frente-negra-brasileira-honra.contexto: The Brazilian Black Front, founded in São Paulo in 1931, was the largest organisation of the Black movement of the period and fought for the social, educational and political inclusion of the Black population.
detalhe: The Lodge’s website reproduces the Folha da Noite column of 13 May 1932 as proof of the “longevity of the memory” of the abolitionists linked to América, especially Worshipful Master Luiz Gama and his ally Antônio Bento, of the Caifazes. The programme included singing the Hymn of the Black People at the tombs and, in the evening, the unveiling of a portrait of José do Patrocínio by the Black artist Olavo Xavier.

In the column, the Black Front’s speaker Vicente Ferreira spoke of the organisation’s work for the “moral and intellectual uplift of the Black race” and promised to carry on “in the breach opened by Patrocínio, Rui Barbosa, Luiz Gama and Castro Alves”, two of them Brethren of América.

1932-a-loja-america-na-revolucao.titulo: América Lodge in the Constitutionalist Revolution
1932-a-loja-america-na-revolucao.texto: América, which in 1931 had issued a manifesto to the Masons of Brazil calling for an immediate return to constitutional rule, supported the Revolution of 1932. Its Brother Pedro de Toledo governed São Paulo during the fighting, members of the Lodge went to the front and the Lodge raised a subscription for the combatants and their families. After the defeat, it approved a vote of disapproval of Grand Master Marrey Júnior, who had begun to say he opposed the movement, and reaffirmed its solidarity with São Paulo.
1932-a-loja-america-na-revolucao.contexto: The Constitutionalist Revolution (9 July to 2 October 1932) demanded from Getúlio Vargas’s Provisional Government a new Constitution and a “civilian and paulista” intervenor. Without the expected support of Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, São Paulo fought alone for almost three months. Defeated militarily, the movement contributed to the election of the Constituent Assembly in 1933 and to the Constitution of 1934.
detalhe: The 1931 manifesto. In February 1931, a few months after the Revolution of 1930, the Lodge issued a manifesto “to the Masons of Brazil”, transcribed in the minutes on 11 March on the proposal of Paulo de Gusmão. The text called for an immediate return to constitutional rule, a new electoral law and new voter registration, the calling of a constituent assembly within six months and the end of the Special Revolutionary Tribunal, and also defended secular education and civil marriage. Lodges in São Paulo, Pernambuco and other states acknowledged receipt and declared their solidarity. In May 1931 Cyro de Souza e Silva was elected Worshipful Master.

A Brother in government. In March 1932, answering the call for a “civilian and paulista” intervenor, Vargas appointed Ambassador Pedro de Toledo, a Brother of América and former Grand Master of the State Grand Orient (1908–1914). According to José Castellani’s article reproduced on the Lodge’s website, the movement’s preparatory meetings were held at the offices of O Estado de S. Paulo, a newspaper founded in 1875 by Masons, among them Américo de Campos and Francisco Rangel Pestana, both of América. On 10 July, a day after the uprising, Pedro de Toledo was acclaimed governor by the people, the Army and the State Police (see the next item).

Freemasonry in the fight. According to the Orator Cyro de Souza e Silva, soon after the movement broke out there was a meeting of Worshipful Masters presided over by the state Grand Master, José Adriano Marrey Júnior, who called on the Brethren to support the revolution in order to obtain the swift constitutionalisation of the country. A patriotic battalion was even organised to bear the name “Dr. Marrey Jr.”. As Governor Pedro de Toledo banned politicians’ names for the battalions, it became the “Rio Grande do Norte Battalion”.

The Lodge during the war. América kept meeting in its temple in the Palacete Piratininga, at Praça da Sé, 26, at least on 6 and 20 July and 10 August 1932, and at the session of 20 July it approved a vote of recognition for the Brethren who had gone to the front lines. João Felizardo Júnior fought in the Northern sector, in the Paraíba Valley. Aristides M. de Souza also went to the front and sent from there a letter with greetings to the Brethren, later read in Lodge. Paulo de Gusmão, Senior Warden, supported the movement while on duty in a coastal town. The subscription among the Brethren reached 180$000, which Treasurer Antonio Mucillo topped up with Lodge funds to 200$000, handed to former Worshipful Master João Gallo for the combatants and their families.

The cost of the war. The fighting also weighed on the Lodge’s accounts. The magazine A Maçonaria cancelled the Lodge’s contributions from July to September “because of the Constitutionalist revolution”, and Arthur Barreto de Aguiar obtained from the building’s owners a reduction of one month’s rent on the temple. In December the Lodge voted its grief at the death of Santos-Dumont, which had occurred in July, during the revolution.

The return to sessions and the Marrey Júnior case. At the first session after the defeat, on 23 November 1932, under Worshipful Master Francisco Xavier Paes de Barros Filho, the circular in which Grand Master Marrey Júnior explained his attitude after the revolution was read: in the newspapers he had declared himself opposed to the movement. The Orator Cyro de Souza e Silva recalled the arrest of nine members of the Democratic Party Directorate and of the MMDC Council and asked why, if he opposed the movement, the Grand Master had called on the Brethren to enlist and dragged Freemasonry into it. He declared: “we were, are and always will be against any and every government of force”.

The debate divided the Lodge. João Felizardo Júnior, who had fought, believed Freemasonry should not take a stand on politics. José Del Picchia Filho replied that, without involving itself in politics, Freemasonry would not have influenced Independence, the Republic and Abolition. Arthur Barreto de Aguiar considered the matter to belong to the Assembly of the Grand Orient. Carmello Garcia announced he would not attend sessions while the case was being discussed.

The vote of 30 November. At the next session the Lodge agreed to acknowledge receipt of the circular and to reaffirm its solidarity with São Paulo. By five votes to four it decided to judge the Grand Master’s conduct and, by six votes, with José Julio Scavone and Paulo de Gusmão abstaining, approved “a vote of disapproval” of Marrey Júnior’s attitude, “entirely contrary to the one taken before the outcome of the struggle”. Scavone also proposed a vote of sympathy for all who, Brethren or not, had faced dangers and sacrifices for the constitutionalist ideal. On 7 December, at Cyro’s request, the minutes recorded that Paulo de Gusmão had given the movement his full support.

The echoes. The stance endured. In June 1934, by then Worshipful Master, Cyro de Souza e Silva declared that, true to what he had said after the Revolution of 1932, he would not vote for Marrey Júnior for state Grand Master. In August 1935, on the death of Pedro de Toledo, the Lodge suspended its work in his honour, on the proposal of Arthur Barreto de Aguiar.

1932-pedro-de-toledo-irmao-da.titulo: Pedro de Toledo, Brother of América, governor during the Revolution of 1932
1932-pedro-de-toledo-irmao-da.texto: Ambassador Pedro de Toledo, a Brother of América Lodge and former Grand Master of the State Grand Orient, was appointed “civilian and paulista” intervenor in March 1932 and, when the Constitutionalist Revolution broke out, acclaimed governor of São Paulo on 10 July.
1932-pedro-de-toledo-irmao-da.contexto: The Constitutionalist Revolution (9/7 to 2/10/1932) demanded a new Constitution from Getúlio Vargas. São Paulo fought alone for three months. The Constituent Assembly came in 1933 and the Constitution in 1934.
detalhe: According to an article by José Castellani reproduced on the Lodge’s website, on 3 March 1932, answering the call for a “Civilian and Paulista” leader, Vargas appointed as intervenor Ambassador Pedro de Toledo, Grand Master of the State Grand Orient from 1908 to 1914, who took office on the 7th. The movement’s preparatory meetings were held at the offices of O Estado de S. Paulo, a newspaper founded by Masons of América.

The revolt took to the streets on 9 July. On the 10th Pedro de Toledo was acclaimed governor by the people, the Army and the State Police. With the surrender on 2 October he was deposed and exiled. In November 1933, when greeting the installation of the Constituent Assembly, São Paulo Masons also voted their praise for the return of “Brother Pedro de Toledo, who had been exiled”.

The Lodge’s website sees in the episode the continuity of the defence of a Brazil “governed in obedience to a Constitution and Democratic Laws”. As early as 1931 América had issued a manifesto to the Masons of Brazil calling for an immediate return to constitutional rule.
At América, on 14 August 1935, the Lodge suspended its work as a posthumous tribute to Pedro de Toledo, who had died in July.
The plaque on his portrait in the Lodge’s gallery of Illustrious Masons gives him as Grand Master from 1908 to 1910; Castellani’s article says 1908 to 1914.
papeis: Brother of the Lodge; intervenor and governor of São Paulo in 1932

1934-frente-maconica-contra-o-fascismo.texto: After a first debate on fascism in March, the Lodge holds a special session with visitors from several lodges: Prof. Rodolpho Jorge Hund analyses Italian, German, Brazilian and clerical fascism, and another Brother describes Nazi pressure on the press. An inter-lodge committee to fight the fascist cells is approved, with representatives of América, Ordem e Progresso, Luiz Gama and Roma.
1934-frente-maconica-contra-o-fascismo.contexto: In 1933 Hitler came to power in Germany. In Brazil, the Brazilian Integralist Action, founded in 1932 by Plínio Salgado and inspired by fascism, was growing fast and had a strongly anti-Masonic discourse.

1936-nem-integralismo-nem-comunismo.texto: Under the state of war of 1936, one Brother warns that if integralism wins, Masons will be persecuted as under Nazism and fascism; the Orator concludes: “neither communism nor integralism, but liberty and democracy”. In July, days after the start of the Spanish Civil War, the Lodge votes its grief for the Masons persecuted in Spain.
1936-nem-integralismo-nem-comunismo.contexto: After the communist uprising of November 1935, the Vargas government decreed a state of siege and then a state of war, with mass arrests. In Spain, in July 1936, the military rebelled against the Republic presided over by Manuel Azaña, opening a civil war that would last until 1939.

1936-nova-sede-na-rua-tabatinguera.titulo: A new home on Rua Tabatinguera
1936-nova-sede-na-rua-tabatinguera.texto: The Lodge rents the temple of Loja Amizade at Rua Barão de Tabatinguera, 37-A, and holds its first session there on 28/10/1936. At the same session it decides not to officially invite the lodges linked directly to the Grand Orient of Brazil, regarded as rebels against the state Grand Orient, and votes praise for Armando de Salles Oliveira for a speech in defence of democracy.
1936-nova-sede-na-rua-tabatinguera.contexto: Rua Tabatinguera, in the old centre, was home to several Masonic lodges. In 1936 the former São Paulo governor Armando de Salles Oliveira was preparing to run in the presidential election of 1938, which would not take place because of the Estado Novo coup.

1937-contra-o-integralismo-e-o.texto: Dr. Cyro de Souza e Silva harshly criticises the integralist leader Plínio Salgado and warns the Brethren against extremisms, both the national imitation of fascism and communism. Scavone, Felizardo Junior and Trentim speak in defence of democracy.
1937-contra-o-integralismo-e-o.contexto: In 1937 the presidential campaign planned for 1938 polarised the country between the fascist-inspired Brazilian Integralist Action and the fear of communism, fuelled since the 1935 uprising. A few months later, in November, Getúlio Vargas would close Congress and establish the Estado Novo, initially with integralist support.

1937-as-vesperas-do-estado-novo.titulo: On the eve of the Estado Novo: the shutdown
1937-as-vesperas-do-estado-novo.texto: At the last session before the shutdown, the Lodge expresses solidarity with a lodge in Assis that was calling on Masons to stand against extremism. It is reported that the state Assembly recommended suspending celebrations and keeping a watch on initiations, and that the state Grand Orient banned Masonic meetings and congresses. The Lodge would not meet again until February 1940.
1937-as-vesperas-do-estado-novo.contexto: On 10 November 1937 Getúlio Vargas staged the Estado Novo coup, closed Congress and imposed a new constitution. The regime severely restricted associational and political life, and many Masonic lodges suspended their activities.

1940-reabertura-apos-tres-anos.texto: The Lodge reopens with a grand session after about three years of inactivity, with Worshipful Master Arthur Barreto de Aguiar hailing a new phase of peace for Freemasonry. A month later the Orator laments that only half a dozen Brethren attend. The newly elected Worshipful Master asked for an account of the period without work.
1940-reabertura-apos-tres-anos.contexto: The reopening took place still under the Estado Novo, which lasted until 1945, and at the start of the Second World War. Rebuilding membership was slow in many lodges after the period of inactivity.

1940-a-soberania-da-loja-posta.titulo: The Lodge’s sovereignty put to the test
1940-a-soberania-da-loja-posta.texto: On the eve of the initiation of a candidate already approved by ballot, the Grand Secretariat suspends the ceremony. Jealous of its sovereignty, the Lodge gives Worshipful Master Arlindo Ribeiro a vote of confidence to seek clarification; he considers the case perhaps unprecedented in the annals of São Paulo Freemasonry. At the same session the Lodge celebrates its 72nd anniversary.
1940-a-soberania-da-loja-posta.contexto: Reopened in 1940 under the Estado Novo, Freemasonry worked under surveillance and with redoubled caution in admitting new members. The episode shows the tension between each Lodge’s traditional autonomy and the control of the Obediences in that period.

1942-o-brasil-entra-na-guerra.texto: In April the Lodge transcribes a circular applauding Brazil’s break with Germany, Italy and Japan. In August it holds a minute’s silence for the martyrs of the Brazilian ships torpedoed off the coast of Bahia. A decree banned Axis subjects from attending Masonic meetings, but in October permission arrived for Brethren in that situation to attend again.
1942-o-brasil-entra-na-guerra.contexto: In January 1942 Brazil broke off relations with the Axis. In August German submarines sank several Brazilian merchant ships off the Northeast coast, killing hundreds, and on 22 August the government recognised a state of war with Germany and Italy. German, Italian and Japanese immigrants faced restrictions.

1943-com-os-aliados-da-queda.titulo: With the Allies, from Mussolini’s fall to victory
1943-com-os-aliados-da-queda.texto: In July 1943 the Lodge votes its rejoicing at the fall of fascism in Italy, at the same session in which it receives its founding documents from the GOB; at the 75th anniversary, in November, the Orator stated that the idea of the Free Womb Law had been born in the Lodge. In June 1944 it sends a letter to Franklin Roosevelt congratulating him on the invasion of Europe and, in April 1945, holds a minute’s silence for his death. In July 1945 it celebrates the return of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force.
1943-com-os-aliados-da-queda.contexto: Mussolini was deposed on 25 July 1943. On 6 June 1944 (D-Day) the Allies landed in Normandy. The Brazilian Expeditionary Force fought in Italy in 1944 and 1945 and returned to Brazil in July 1945.

1945-protesto-contra-o-massacre-dos.titulo: Protest against the massacre of the Jews
1945-protesto-contra-o-massacre-dos.texto: On a communication from Loja Rei Salomão, the Lodge records a protest against the massacre of Jews committed by the Nazis, with a vote of grief and a minute’s silence. It is one of the first mentions of the Holocaust in the minutes.
1945-protesto-contra-o-massacre-dos.contexto: During the Second World War the Nazi regime murdered some six million Jews. The extermination camps were liberated in 1944 and 1945, and the scale of the genocide became widely known at the end of the war.

1946-redemocratizacao-e-guerra-fria.texto: In 1945 the Orator condemns the “black night of 15 years” and defends voter registration and literacy; in 1946 the Worshipful Master has the Lodge’s rejoicing at the return to constitutional rule with the new Constitution put on record. Soon after, the Lodge calls for calm in the face of the closing of the Communist Party (1947) and is divided over the stripping of the communist deputies’ mandates (1948).
1946-redemocratizacao-e-guerra-fria.contexto: Vargas was deposed in October 1945 and the new Constitution was promulgated in September 1946. With the start of the Cold War, the registration of the Communist Party of Brazil was revoked in 1947 and its parliamentarians’ mandates in January 1948.

1954-o-edificio-sede-da-rua.titulo: The headquarters building on Rua São Joaquim
1954-o-edificio-sede-da-rua.texto: The minutes follow the construction of the headquarters building of the Grand Orient of São Paulo, to which the lodges contributed, and record in March 1954 the transfer of the obedience’s bodies to Rua São Joaquim. According to the survey of meeting places, América Lodge met in the GOSP Headquarters Building, at Rua São Joaquim, 457, until September 1972.
1954-o-edificio-sede-da-rua.contexto: The 1950s were years of expansion and institutionalisation for São Paulo Freemasonry, which gained a palace of its own in the Liberdade district. In 1954 São Paulo celebrated its Fourth Centenary and consolidated its position as the country’s largest city.

1954-a-morte-de-getulio-vargas.texto: Elias Rahal asks for a minute’s silence for the death of President Getúlio Vargas. The Orator, although he considers it too early to judge the former president, supports the tribute, and the Secretary speaks about Masonic tolerance, a sign of the division of opinion in the Lodge.
1954-a-morte-de-getulio-vargas.contexto: On 24 August 1954, under pressure from a serious political and military crisis, Getúlio Vargas killed himself in the Catete Palace. His death caused popular commotion and postponed the crisis that would return in 1955.

1954-contra-a-exclusao-dos-estrangeiros.texto: The Lodge approves an opinion that foreign-born Brethren may be elected state Grand Master, after a debate in which one Brother warns of the dangers of nationalism. In 1936, by contrast, a Worshipful Master-elect of foreign origin had judged that the office should go to a Brazilian. In the 1940s and 1950s the Lodge’s leadership already included many members of Syrian-Lebanese origin.
1954-contra-a-exclusao-dos-estrangeiros.contexto: São Paulo received large waves of Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Syrian-Lebanese, Japanese and other immigrants. The nationalism of the Vargas period imposed restrictions on foreigners, a debate that also ran through Freemasonry.

1962-brasilia-e-a-crise-dos.texto: Worshipful Master Miguel Attie reports on a visit to Brasília, where a Masonic temple was being built on land donated by the Federal Government, a project to which the Lodge contributed. At the same session the Orator condemns the arming of Cuba by the Soviet Union. The following year the Lodge would comment on the assassination of President Kennedy.
1962-brasilia-e-a-crise-dos.contexto: Brasília was inaugurated in 1960. In October 1962 the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba brought the United States and the Soviet Union to the brink of nuclear war, at the tensest moment of the Cold War.

1964-o-golpe-de-1964.texto: In March the Lodge debates the basic reforms, and one Brother defends unionisation of rural workers but criticises the president’s methods. At the first session after 31 March, Brethren celebrate the overthrow of the Goulart government; the Orator speaks of a “bloodless coup” but recalls revolutions that lost their way and calls for the victory of peace. On 15/04 the Lodge proposes solidarity with General Amaury Kruel and Marshal Castelo Branco, with one dissenting voice.
1964-o-golpe-de-1964.contexto: On 31 March and 1 April 1964 a civil-military coup deposed President João Goulart, who advocated basic reforms such as land reform. Marshal Castelo Branco took over the Presidency, beginning a military regime that would last until 1985.

1968-luto-por-martin-luther-king.texto: Miguel Attié proposes a vote of grief for the assassination of Martin Luther King, recalling that the hundred-year-old Lodge had the freeing of the slaves as its hallmark. At the same session the committee on the Lodge’s history asks for contributions and photos for the centenary.
1968-luto-por-martin-luther-king.contexto: Martin Luther King Jr., leader of the civil rights movement of the Black population in the United States and winner of the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize, was assassinated on 4 April 1968 in Memphis.

1968-o-centenario-da-loja.texto: The Lodge celebrates its centenary on 9 November 1968, inviting the highest dignitaries of Brazilian Freemasonry, with a joint session with Loja Luiz Gama and a session on Freemasonry in Brazilian history. It receives messages from state Grand Masters and from the GOB’s Supreme Court, and the national Grand Master confers on it the title of “Grand Benefactress” and the “Star of Masonic Distinction”. At the same time, the minutes record a GOB act on expelling members for ideologies contrary to the Order.
1968-o-centenario-da-loja.contexto: The centenary came in the tensest year of the military regime: in December 1968 Institutional Act No. 5 closed Congress and suspended constitutional guarantees. Around the world, 1968 was marked by student protests and social movements.

1969-do-rito-escoces-ao-rito.titulo: From the Scottish Rite to the Brazilian Rite
1969-do-rito-escoces-ao-rito.texto: In a roll-call vote, the Lodge approves by 12 votes to 6, with 2 abstentions, leaving the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, in which it had been founded, and adopting the Brazilian Rite. The change was authorised by the GOB in 1970, with a new Charter; opponents such as Alfeu Diniz da Silva asked to leave. The first initiation in the new rite was that of Asclepíades Jesus Borges de Lemos, whom the plaque records as Worshipful Master in 1995–1997.
1969-do-rito-escoces-ao-rito.contexto: Rites are the systems of ceremonies and degrees that each lodge practises. The Brazilian Rite, created in Brazil in the twentieth century with a strong civic and patriotic character, gained followers in the 1960s and 1970s.
fotos: The Charter of the Grand Orient of Brazil of 23 July 1970, which regularises “América, Brazilian Rite” as Symbolic Lodge América No. 189.

1971-acusada-de-nucleo-comunista.texto: Worshipful Master Assad Mogames announces that the state Grand Master has accused América Lodge and two others of being “communist cells”, and asks the Lodge’s representative to lodge a protest and a defence. In July a Brother reports that the Grand Master, commenting on a complaint against himself to the DOPS political police, cited América among the lodges said to harbour extremists. The accusation worsened the friction between the Lodge and the state Grand Orient.
1971-acusada-de-nucleo-comunista.contexto: In the early 1970s, under the Médici government, political repression reached its peak, and the DOPS (Department of Political and Social Order) investigated people and organisations suspected of opposition. An accusation of communism could have serious consequences.

1972-ruptura-com-o-grande-oriente.titulo: Break with the São Paulo Grand Orient
1972-ruptura-com-o-grande-oriente.texto: In the crisis between the Grand Orient of Brazil and that of São Paulo, the Lodge approves the “Proclamation to Masons” on the side of the GOB and decides not to comply with the decree of the suspended Grand Master Danilo José Fernandes suspending its officers, burning it “out of fidelity to our oaths”. It is prepared to meet outside the Headquarters Building if prevented from entering. In 1973 it prints for the whole country the “Rendering of Accounts”, its version of the split, and refuses to follow the new obedience created by Danilo.
1972-ruptura-com-o-grande-oriente.contexto: In 1972 and 1973 a serious crisis in the Grand Orient of Brazil led several state Grand Orients to separate and form independent obediences. In São Paulo the dispute divided lodges, Brethren and Masonic property itself.

1972-fora-do-edificio-sede-santo.titulo: Away from the Headquarters Building: Santo Amaro and the dream of a temple of its own
1972-fora-do-edificio-sede-santo.texto: Removed from the Headquarters Building, the Lodge begins meeting in the temple lent by Loja Francisco Glicério in Santo Amaro, and appoints a committee to draw up a plan for a temple of its own. In 1973 it creates a Property Fund to raise money for the building, a subject that returns to the minutes in 1974.
1972-fora-do-edificio-sede-santo.contexto: Santo Amaro, a former municipality incorporated into São Paulo in 1935, was growing fast with the industrialisation of the South Zone. Having a temple of their own was a long-standing aspiration of many lodges, which for decades met in rented or borrowed premises.

1974-saudacao-a-revolucao-dos-cravos.texto: A Brother asks for a vote of rejoicing at the fall of the dictatorship in Portugal. At the same session the Orator asks for a study on Luiz Gama, “our W∴M∴”, and action is demanded on the temple and the centenary golden book.
1974-saudacao-a-revolucao-dos-cravos.contexto: On 25 April 1974 a military movement in Portugal overthrew the authoritarian regime established by Salazar, in place since the 1930s. The Carnation Revolution opened the way to Portuguese democracy and to the independence of the African colonies.

1975-ultimo-registro-do-acervo.texto: In October and November 1974 the Lodge follows decisions of the São Paulo Court of Appeal rejecting appeals by Samuel José Fernandes in the dispute over possession of the Masonic headquarters, and rejects the proposals for reconciliation with the dissidents. In the archive’s last minutes, on 12/03/1975, the Orator comments on a notice by Samuel José Fernandes in the newspapers asserting the regularity of his Grand Orient at Rua São Joaquim, 457, and the Worshipful Master announces a dinner with former president Jânio Quadros.
1975-ultimo-registro-do-acervo.contexto: The 1973 division between São Paulo Masonic obediences lasted a long time and left its mark on the organisation of Freemasonry in the state. In 1975 Brazil was under the Geisel government and at the start of the slow political “opening”.

1975-1975-a-hoje-os-veneraveis.titulo: 1975 to today: the Worshipful Masters on the plaque
1975-1975-a-hoje-os-veneraveis.texto: The minutes after 1975 have not yet been added to the digital archive; for this period the source is the plaque of Worshipful Masters. It records Otaviano Dias Ferreira Lopes (1975–1977), Assad Mogames (1977–1979), Júlio Chagas do Nascimento (1979–1981, 1985–1987 and 1999–2003), Heitor Genta, Pedro Abrahão, Oswaldo Melantonio, Antonio Paraguassú Lopes, Merson Mohamed Nór, Edgard Afif Chehin, Asclepíades Jesus Borges de Lemos, Gumercindo Rúbio de Souza, Fernando Baptistton Scalabrin, José Luis Carmanhães, Orlando de Lemos Falcone Junior, Wagner Ricardo Odri, Mauro Tippi, Pascoal Nicola Giantomasi, Kiyoshi Tsumura, Alvimar Sanches de Magalhães Júnior, Paulo Luiz Maximiliano and Luciano Gebara David, up to José Carlos Gomes de Oliveira (2025–2027). Several of them already appear in the minutes of the 1960s and 1970s as officers or newly initiated members.
1975-1975-a-hoje-os-veneraveis.contexto: Over these five decades Brazil went through redemocratisation, the 1988 Constitution and profound social change, and Brazilian Freemasonry remained organised in different obediences. The Lodge’s history in this period can be told in detail once its minutes are added to the archive.

2006-nasce-o-instituto-herdeiros-do.titulo: The Instituto Herdeiros do Futuro is born
2006-nasce-o-instituto-herdeiros-do.texto: On the evening of 28/08/2006, Volunteer Day, 23 people met in the social hall of América Lodge and founded the Instituto Herdeiros do Futuro (Heirs of the Future Institute), on the initiative of the Lodge’s Brethren. The institute offers free social, psychological, educational and legal support to child victims of violence and their families, to break the cycle of domestic violence.
2006-nasce-o-instituto-herdeiros-do.contexto: Today the institute runs six units of the Social Protection Service for Child and Adolescent Victims of Violence (SPVV) in São Paulo’s South Zone, in partnership with the city government, and reports more than 35,000 people assisted.
detalhe: On the evening of 28 August 2006, Volunteer Day, 23 people met in the social hall of América Lodge and signed the founding minutes of the Instituto Herdeiros do Futuro. They were Brethren of the Lodge, their wives and friends. The Lodge was led by Worshipful Master Fernando Baptistton Scalabrin (2005–2007).

The attendance list of the founding minutes was signed by: Régis Fernando Ferreira, Mauro Tippi, Aldo Zerbini, Gil Lourenço de Freitas, Ricardo Gonçalves, Fernando Scalabrin, Pascoal Giantomasi, José Carneiro Nascimento, Marcio Gaba, Gislene Magalhães, Suzi Gaba, Alvimar Magalhães Jr., Amadeu Gonçales Filho, Francisco Silveira Mello, Maria Tereza Gonçales, José Teruo Mizuno, Heitor Genta, Edel Carmanhães, José Luis Carmanhães, Alexandre Petri, Luciano Correa and Célia Petri. Bro∴ Wagner Odri presided over the institute.

Several of these Brethren would later lead the Lodge itself: José Luis Carmanhães (2007–2009), Wagner Ricardo Odri (2011–2013), Mauro Tippi (2013–2015), Pascoal Nicola Giantomasi (2015–2017) and Alvimar Sanches de Magalhães Júnior (2019–2021).

The IHF began in Santo Amaro, with free psychological and social care for child victims of violence and their families. By 2008 it had provided more than 800 consultations. By 2019 it had already benefited more than 20,000 people, invested some R$ 16 million of public and private funds and created 45 direct jobs. It is run on a voluntary basis by the Lodge’s members.
